en: Having heard this, Mahāśvetā reflected for a long time and, saying, "Go;
I shall come in person and act as is appropriate," she dispatched Keyūraka.
And having gone, Keyūraka said to Candrāpīḍa: “Prince,
Hemakūṭa is delightful,
and the capital city of Citraratha is wonderful.”
The realm of the Kimpuruṣas is full of many wonders; the world of the Gandharvas is charming;
and Kādambarī is both simple-hearted and noble-minded.
When you perceive the journey as not being overly fatiguing, when the important task does not falter,
and when the mind is curious about objects never seen before;

Whether you follow my words or [my] speech, it would be a source of happiness; or rather, your thought [being] exceedingly pleasant would be a sight of wonder, and I am worthy of this affection, or you ought to grant me this request.
Do you consider me unworthy of being rejected, or do you consider me worthy? Do you perceive that even a slight degree of intimacy has been established,
or that this person is one who should be favored?

Therefore, you ought not to render this request of mine fruitless. Come with me to Hemakūṭa, the repository of exquisite beauty; having gone there, you shall behold Kādambarī, who is no different from myself.
"Setting aside this evil thought, which is but a play of mental delusion, rest for one day; on the morrow you shall return.
For, upon seeing you—a friend without cause—my heart, though long overwhelmed by the weight of the darkness of sorrow, feels as if it has finally drawn a deep breath."
"Having heard this account of my own life, my grief has become as if bearable;

for the company of the virtuous delights even those who are suffering, and the arising of virtues in those such as yourself is dependent upon bringing happiness to others. To her, as she spoke thus, Candrāpīḍa replied: "Blessed Lady!"
"From this moment on, this person is at your disposal; please command me as you wish in whatever needs to be done," she said, and set out together with her.

Traveling by degrees, they reached Hemakūṭa, the palace of the Gandharva king; passing through seven inner courtyards adorned with golden archways, she arrived at the gate of the princess's inner apartments.

Being shown the way by a group of doorkeepers and female attendants who ran forward upon seeing Mahāśvetā, carrying golden cane-staffs in their hands and offering salutations from afar, he entered a place crowded with hundreds of thousands of countless women—
a second world of living beings composed entirely of women.
As if the female population of the three worlds had been gathered together in one place to grasp its full extent;
as if it were another creation devoid of men; as if an unprecedented island of women had come into being.
Like a fifth incarnation of the pair of women from the *Yuga*, like another creation by the Creator who hates men,
it was as if a treasury of women had been produced and established for the sake of fashioning many kalpas.
With an exceedingly vast flood of the radiance of the beauty of young women that inundated the horizons, as if sprinkling the world with a stream of nectar-essence,
and raining down abundant splendor, the entire interior of the universe seemed, by being encompassed on all sides, as if composed of light, as if made of emerald gems.
Its structure was as if fashioned from thousands of lunar discs;
its arrangement was as if constructed from moonlight;
and the quarters of space were as if produced by the radiance of its ornaments.
It was as if all its furnishings had been fashioned by delusions;
its limbs were as if produced by the playful charms of youth; and its accumulation [of parts] was as if constructed by the amorous dalliances of Rati.
It seemed as if it had been fashioned with space provided by the movements of the God of Love;
its every region appeared as if anointed with passion, as if consisting entirely of erotic sentiment,
and as if composed of nothing but beauty.
As if composed of the presiding deities of love, as if composed of the flower-arrowed god,
and as if composed of curiosity.
The prince beheld the interior of the maidens' quarters as if it were composed of wonder, as if composed of tenderness, and as if composed of love.
And because that multitude of maidens was so densely packed, there seemed to be a rain of moon-discs falling from all sides from the rivers of their faces;
by the casting of their sidelong glances, the earth was being made as if composed of groves of swaying blue water-lilies;
and by the playful movements of their unsteady creeper-like eyebrows, hundreds of charms of Kama’s bow were, as it were, manifested.
Hundreds of graceful movements were set in motion,
as if forming caravans for the night of the dark fortnight through the darkness of their clusters of lotus-like hair.
Moving about with the radiance of their smiles, they made the days of spring appear as if white with full-blown flowers;
wandering with the fragrance of their sighs, they made the Malaya breezes seem to be circling about;

with the glow from the circles of their cheeks, they made thousands of ruby mirrors flash forth; and by the redness of their palms, they made the world of living beings seem as if it were raining down groves of red lotuses.
The quarters of the sky were covered, as it were, by thousands of arrows of the flower-armed god through the flashing of the rays from her fingernails;
and the flocks of peacocks in the palace seemed to take flight with the masses of rays from her ornaments, which resembled a network of rainbows.
He beheld as it were thousands of Love-gods being brought forth by the transformations of youth:
under the pretext of customary activities, he saw the taking of hands in the form of young maidens grasping the hands of their friends,
and kisses in the form of flute-playing.
The movements of her fingernails upon the lutes,
the strikes of her palms during ball games, the embraces of her vine-like arms around the necks of the water-jars used for sprinkling the creepers of the palace grounds,
and the swaying of her hips and breasts upon the pleasure-swing;

In some places the word "tāmbūla" is not seen; [therein are described] the services of the teeth in the breaking of betel rolls, and the pouring of mouthfuls of honey upon *bakula* branches— [in other versions, the pouring of mouthfuls of *sīdhu* wine during the longing for *bakula* flowers]—
and the striking with feet upon the *aśoka* trees.

He saw [them] practicing, as it were, an extraordinary form of lovemaking through the *sītkāra* sounds produced when their offerings of flowers stumbled; and among those young maidens, the mere light upon the surface of their cheeks served as the washing of their faces,
and their very eyes served as the blue lotuses for their ears.
Her very complexion was her cosmetic ointment;
her breaths were her application of perfumes;
the luster of her lips was her saffron face-paste; and her conversations were the resonance of her lute strings.
Her creeper-like arms were indeed garlands of *campaka* flowers;
her palms were indeed playful lotuses; and her breasts were indeed mirrors.

The very luster of her own body served as her veil of fine silk; the floors of her birthplace were themselves the jeweled slabs for her amorous play; the color of the tender soles of her feet was her very lac-dye for her feet; and the rays from the jewels of her nails were the heaps of flowers offered upon the mosaic pavements.
And in that place, even the juice of lac upon her feet was a burden too heavy for her steps; even the wearing of a girdle of *bakula* garlands was an obstacle to her movement;
and even the weight of her body-unguents became a cause for excessive panting.
Even a burden of fine garments causes exhaustion;
even the wearing of auspicious *pratisara* amulets and bracelets is a cause for the trembling of the palms;
and even the wearing of flowers as ear-ornaments is a source of fatigue.

Even the breeze from the wings of the bees hovering over the lotuses adorning her ears causes her distress; likewise, where rising with the support of a friend’s hand upon being seen is considered an act of extreme rashness,
and the ability to bear the weight of necklaces during adornment is attributed to the power of the firmness of her breasts.

In the gathering of flowers, even the grasping of a second flower is unbecoming for one who is not young; in the arts of maidens, the weaving of garlands is an occupation for those who are not delicate;
and in prostrations before deities, the breaking of the waist is not very surprising.

And as he, being of such a nature, having entered the interior and moved a short distance further inside, was wandering here and there near Kādambarī’s attendants, he overheard their various most enchanting conversations, such as this: “Lavalikā!
Prepare circles for the basins of the lavalī creepers with the pollen of ketaka flowers.”
<2> <2.sārasike> Sāgarika, [scatter] the jewel-sand upon the lotus ponds and the golden streams <3> <3.gandhodakadīrghikāsu, kanakanadikāsu> of the fragrant water.
Mṛṇālikā, sprinkle artificial lotus ponds with handfuls of saffron powder; Makarikā, [place] pairs of mechanical cakravāka birds here and there. Mandārikā... [do the same].

"Rajanike, scent the incense-burners with the juice of camphor sprouts. Nighe, place the jewel-lamps within the darkness of the tamāla avenues and the ponds of the palace. Kumudike, cover [the fruits] with nets of pearls for the sake of protection, against the flocks of birds. Nipuṇike, [place] the pomegranate fruits."
<11> <11.lekhaya> Write [this]. <12> <12.maṇistambhā...> O Utpalika, apply patterns of saffron juice on the breasts of the jeweled statues on the jeweled pillars;
wipe the emerald pedestal of the plantain bower with golden brooms. <1> <1.kamalasammārjanībhiḥ, saṃmārjanībhiḥ> <2> <2.vedikāḥ> [Use] lotus-brooms and brooms.
O Kesarike! O Kusumike!
Sprinkle the Bakula-flower garland-houses with the essence of wine.
O Malatike! Paint the ivory balconies of the temple of Kamadeva with vermilion powder.
Nalinikā, feed the domestic kalahamsa geese with the sweet nectar of lotuses. Kadali, lead the house peacocks to the fountain-house. Kamalini—
"Give the juice of lotus-stalks and milk to the young ruddy geese and to the geese;
O mango-creeper, give food consisting of fresh buds and sprouts to the male cuckoos in their cages."
Pallavikā, feed the domestic mynahs with sprouts of black pepper. Lavaṅgikā, scatter pieces of long-pepper and rice in the cages of the cakora birds.
Madhukarikā—
"Mayūrikā, fashion the flower ornaments! Kandalikā, release the pairs of kinnaras into the music hall! Release the pairs of jīvañjīva birds onto the peak of the pleasure mountain!"

"Harimikā! Give me instruction for the parrots and mynahs. [8] ...[the instruction for the mynahs]... he heard these and other such playful remarks, as follows: "Cāmarike! What do you wish to deceive by manifesting false innocence? [1] [1. in vain]...

O you who have been made intoxicated by the charms of youth, you are recognized—you who, with your form bent down by the weight of your jar-like breasts, lean against the peacocks atop the jeweled pillars. (Or: ...lean against the rays of the jeweled pillars.)
O you who desire jesting,
you converse with your own reflection fallen upon the jeweled wall— you converse with a mere image— while your upper garment has been carried away by the wind.
With the palm of your hand whitened by the luster of your necklace, you gather [the reflections]; fearing the stumbling of the offering lotuses upon the jeweled floors,
you avoid the reflections of your own face.

[She], whose innate delicacy eclipses the beauty of the lotus stalk, [is] apprehensive of the morning sunlight regarding the light of rubies fallen through the lattice-windows. (Note: In some versions, the portion beginning with "nijasaukumārya... up to "jāla" is not found; furthermore, in other versions, the word ending in the vocative case is not seen at all.)
You hold the palm of your hand over [your head] like a parasol;
with your hand drooping from exhaustion,
the fly-whisk has slipped from your grasp.
Even as he heard these and other such words—“you shake the mass of rays from your moon-like nails”—he approached the vicinity of Kādambarī’s palace. Having reached the palace, he proceeded;
having approached the palace, he went [inside]. The grounds were like a sandy bank due to the masses of flower-dust fallen from the creepers of the grove.
[The garden] appeared like a foul day with showers of mango-fruit juice from women whose limbs were marked by the scratches of the nails of silent cuckoos;
it resembled a mist with the scattered, dark dust from the streams of *sīdhu* wine poured upon the *vakula* trees;
and it took on the appearance of the Golden Isle (*kāñcanadvīpa*) with offerings of *campaka* petals.
It resembled a grove of blue *aśoka* trees due to the darkness created by swarms of bees falling upon the heaps of flowers;
likewise, it acted as an ocean of passion for the women moving about because of the spreading streams of red lac from their feet,
and it resembled the day of the birth of the nectar of immortality because of the fragrance of their body-unguents.

It resembled the world of the moon with the circles of radiance from its ānanda-leaf ornaments; it appeared like a grove of *priyaṅgu* trees with decorative leaf-patterns of black agallochum (*kṛṣṇāguru*); it was like a forest of *priyaṅgu* with the application of yellow pigment (*rocanā*) tilaka marks;
and it appeared blue-black with decorative leaf-patterns of black agallochum.
It was turning red with ear-ornaments of *aśoka* sprouts,
white with ointments of sandalwood paste,
and green with *śirīṣa* flower ornaments.
Then he saw a road that had been fashioned into the shape of a long street by a multitude of women who had come for the sake of service and were standing on both sides like a wall made of beauty;
and he beheld the massed light of the rays from their ornaments falling within it, flowing together like a stream of water in a river's eddy.
And having proceeded through its midst as if against the current, he beheld a glorious pavilion at its front, its forepart occupied by a circle of female door-keepers.

And there, in the center, she was surrounded by a multitude of thousands of young maidens seated upon a circular arrangement (*maṇḍala*) below, some seated within the *maṇḍala*, and others seated above the *maṇḍala*; they were like a cluster of wish-fulfilling creepers (*kalpalatā*), their masses of ornaments shimmering. She sat before a not very large [object] covered by a canopy of blue silk cloth. [In some versions, the word "not" (*na ati*) is not seen.]
In some places, only the phrase "of the exceedingly great" is seen; [she was] resting upon the support of her couch,
leaning with the support of her twin creeper-like arms placed upon white pillows—
resembling the earth supported by the tusks of a great boar.
She was being fanned by fly-whisk bearers who seemed to be swimming through the water of the spreading network of light from her body with the tossing movements of their creeper-like arms;
she appeared to be carried away by the *nāgas* beneath her upon the jeweled pavements due to the falling of her reflection,
led away individually by the world-protectors (*dikpālas*) against the jeweled walls at her sides, and lifted up by the immortals (*amaras*) within the jeweled pavilions above.
She seemed to have been drawn into the very heart by the great jeweled pillars;
she was as if swallowed by the mirrors of the palace;
and with the host of Vidyādharas scattered beneath her in the middle of the glorious pavilion, she appeared as if about to ascend to the vault of heaven.

She was surrounded by the three worlds, as it were, gathered together out of curiosity to behold her under the pretext of viewing her paintings; she was being gazed upon with unblinking eyes by her own attendants— who, like the palace itself adorned with variegated moon-patterns, seemed to have acquired a thousand eyes through wonder,
or as if they had gained divine vision out of a longing to see her.
With all her limbs presided over by the primary marks as if they were possessed by passion, she seemed to be casting off her childhood state as if it were something devoid of merit.
Though not given away, she was as if being seized by youth, which had become subject to the possession of the god of love;
she was adorned with the radiance of the red dye on her feet that seemed to have issued forth, or like streams of the water of beauty flowing down,
reddened by the juice of lac-dye.

[Her feet] were endowed with toes that, through their exceedingly delicate grace, seemed to discharge showers of blood from the gaps between the nails— as if with crests of red silk from her garment hanging down like flames, and creating the illusion of streaks of red silk from her foot-ornaments.
She was setting in motion with her two feet a river of coral juice, while her circle of jewel-like nails bore upon them a multitude of stars upon the surface of the earth;
she was accompanied by a pair of thighs exhausted by the weight of her heavy hips, which were encircled by the halo of rays from the jewels in her anklets.

Her hips were touched by his rising [hand] as if to provide assistance; and from the region of her waist, which had been firmly pressed by the hand of Prajāpati, a stream of loveliness flowed down due to its impact against the surface of the stone of her hips.
She possessed a pair of thighs that appeared as if split in two;
she seemed to block the sight of other men with the circle of her long, outstretched rays on all sides,
to expand her own curiosity, and to shed a thrill of horripilation through the pleasure of touch.
Her hips were encircled by a girdle of golden bells;
her buttocks were exceedingly heavy, as if burdened by the weight of the hearts of all the world fallen upon them;
and the region of her waist was diminishing, as if from the pain of not being able to see her face because it was concealed by her high breasts.

Because of the extreme delicacy of Prajāpati’s touch, she bore a whorled navel-sculpture that appeared as if it were indented by a finger-ring; she possessed a sprout-like line of body hair, as if it were an inscription of the letters of the panegyric for his conquest of the three worlds, written by the God of Love.

She possessed two thighs that appeared as if split in two by a stream of loveliness flowing from her waist— squeezed firm by Prajāpati— and which, having fallen from there, were diverted by the impact against the stone surface of her hips;
she seemed to be obstructing the sight of other men out of jealousy with a circle of long, spreading rays extended in every direction.
Her orb-like hips were encircled by a girdle that, as if spreading out through curiosity, seemed to extend her form; and as if shedding horripilation through the pleasure of touch,
it was exceedingly heavy, as though bearing the weight of the hearts of all the world fallen upon them.
Her waist appeared to diminish as if from the pain of not being able to see her face, which was hidden between her high breasts;
she bore a whorled navel-sculpture that seemed indented by the finger-prints of Prajāpati as he touched it out of extreme tenderness.
She bore a line of downy hair like a row of blossoms written by the God of Love as a panegyric of his victory over the three worlds;

she was adorned with a fullness of breasts that resembled the footstool of the fish-bannered god, which seemed to be emerging as it were, driven by the palms of her heart— oppressed by its own excessive weight— as it reflected the image of the leaf-like ear-ornaments that had entered within.

She was illuminated by her two arms, which were like stainless lotus stalks of pure luster extending forth as if from the rays of her downward-hanging ear-ornaments; and she was graced by her pair of hands, which, raining down a multitude of rays from her nails, seemed to emit a lattice of sweat-drops due to the fatigue of supporting the weight of her ruby bracelets.

With her chin held high by her necklace as if lifting up her face, which was being bent down by the weight of her breasts; with lips as red as coral vines, appearing like two waves risen from the ocean of passion agitated by the wind of fresh youth; and with a pair of cheeks possessing a clear, radiant luster, both rosy and pale, resembling the surface of a pair of mussels filled with the essence of wine.
She was radiant with a nose-bridge as beautiful as the jeweled corner of Rati’s lute, and with a pair of eyes that seemed slightly reddened at the corners—

as if out of anger at the obstruction of the expansion of her gait— acting as if they were about to transform the world of living beings into a realm consisting solely of eyes, for those eyes were a milky ocean that served as the dwelling place for the splendor of her own face.

She wore a pair of earrings consisting of emerald and ruby, adorned with swinging leaf-patterns and sea-monsters; they were like two streaks of rut from the elephant of her intoxicating youth, or like two hearts of passion drawn with red arsenic paste and fixed upon her face. She bore an earring-lasso that, with its ornament of a single attached gold fillet, caused one to suspect it was a stream of honey falling from a blue lotus released from her ear.

With her forehead made crimson by the crest-jewel kissing the parting of her hair, she seemed to have her long tresses washed with the liquid essence of wine—the spreading mass of rays from that jewel;

she displayed a special excellence of beauty shown by the God of Love who had entered her every limb, as if out of a desire to conquer Gaurī, who was proud because half of her body had been entered by Śiva; and she appeared to possess hundreds of Lakṣmīs through their reflections, as if to remove the pride of Nārāyaṇa, who was delighted by having Lakṣmī alone placed upon his chest.

She seemed to cast thousands of moons in every direction with her playful smiles to destroy the pride of Śiva, who was astonished by the single moon resting upon his head; she appeared to create tens of thousands of Love-gods in every heart out of anger toward the Lord of Spirits, who had mercilessly consumed the one God of Love; and for the sake of sleep, she fashioned little sandbanks of lotus-pollen dust in the pleasure-pools for the pairs of cakravāka birds, who were weary from keeping watch through the night.

She was commanding the female keeper of the swans, saying, "Bring here the pair of swans that have departed with the low murmur of their attendants— the beloved pair, so difficult to find, who have set out together"—
while she herself licked the rays of emerald from her ornaments.

In one place, she was honoring the female gardener— who had come to announce the first emergence of flowers from the creeper she herself had nurtured— by bestowing upon her all her ornaments, after having removed the spreading barley sprouts that were being eaten by the fawns of the palace deer out of greed for the tips of the green grass-blades, as she had heard from her friends.

She was repeatedly making the playful mountain— a cause for laughter due to her unintelligible speech— speak with a leaf-cup filled with various forest flowers and fruits she had brought; she was conversing with the female Śabara of the mountain,
who was being struck by her palm and repeatedly leaping up, while [the girl] herself was repeatedly striking back as they retreated and advanced.
She was playing with bees, which were blinded by the fragrance of her breath as if they were blue balls or blue jackets;
she laughed mockingly at a female parrot in its cage who uttered a harsh cry upon hearing her voice, and as she struck the bird on the head with a toy lotus,
the reflection of her pearl-inlaid crescent-shaped ornament fell upon the drops of perspiration.
With the intention of leaving nail-marks covered by a lattice of lines, she struck the bearer of the betel-box on her breast (*payodhara*) with a handful of scented powder; meanwhile,
the reflection of her jeweled earring on the circle of fresh tooth-marks [on his chest] raised the suspicion that it was a dense cluster of new nail-marks.

She was smiling as she covered her cheek with a sprout from her own ear-ornament, which she had given under the pretext of a favor to the female chowrie-bearer; she resembled the Earth when the burden of great mountain-kings had been removed, resting upon the remaining coils of Śeṣa, the best of serpents;
and like the beauty of the spring month, she had the dust from her feet greyed by the pollen of flowers being gathered away by swarms of bees.
It was like the autumn season, having dispelled the pride of the peacocks by the cries of birds whose wings were born from the stirred-up mind;
it was like Gaurī, with her head adorned by white garments;
and it was like a line of forest on the ocean shore, where the thickets of *tāla* trees were as dark as swarms of bees.
She was like the form of the Moon, having taken as his noble wife the personification of unrestrained amorous play;
she was like a forest grove, its center adorned by pale and dark *valī* creepers;
and she was like the beauty of the dawn, her ornaments consisting of rubies pierced by the rays of the sun.
Her thighs, as tender as lotus stalks, were visible against her clear garment like a lotus-plant in the sky;
she possessed the shimmering beauty of moon-stones in the form of the heavy plumage kissing her hips, like a row of peacocks;
and she was like a branch of the wish-fulfilling tree, bestowing the fruits of desire.
<1> <Near the front> seated facing him near the bed: "Who is he?
Whose offspring is he?
Or what is his name?"
What is his appearance like,
what is his age,
and what does he say?
"What did you say to him?
For how long have you known him, and how did this acquaintance with Mahāśvetā come about?"

He beheld Kādambarī, who was repeatedly questioning Keyūraka—whose speech was rendered eloquent by descriptions of her own form—asking, "Will he come here? and whose conversation was entirely centered on Candrāpīḍa. As soon as he beheld the beauty of the crescent moon of Kādambarī’s face, his heart overflowed with nectar like the ocean.
And this thought arose in his mind: "Why did the Creator not make my remaining senses also composed of eyes?
Or what pure deed has been performed by this eye, that it beholds her without restraint?"
Aha! How wonderful is this that has been created by the Creator—a singular abode of all that is beautiful!
From where were these atoms of supreme form obtained?
Surely they must have come from the drops of tears that fell from his pair of eyes due to the pain of the Creator’s touch upon his palms while fashioning them.
As he was thinking, "These forests of kumudas, kamalas, kuvalayas, and saugandhikas have arisen in the world," his eye fell upon her pair of eyes [and then] upon her face.
At that moment, she too, thinking, "Surely this is he whom Keyūraka announced," was smiling with wonder at the sight of his extraordinary beauty.

His gaze, fixed immovably upon her as its target, fell for a long time; and Candrāpīḍa, white-washed by the radiance of her eyes yet overwhelmed by the sight of Kādambarī, shone at that moment like a mountain (or, like Balarāma). And upon seeing her, first there arose a thrill of his hair.
Then followed the sound of her ornaments,
and immediately after that, Kādambarī rose up;
then it was the flower-weaponed god himself who caused perspiration to arise upon her.
The exertion of rising up in agitation became a mere pretext;
the very great trembling of her thighs obstructed her progress,
and she incurred the disgrace of attracting flocks of swans by the sound of her anklets.
The very movement of her sighs caused her garment to flutter;
the breeze from the yak-tail fans became merely a pretext.
As if out of a longing for the touch of Candrāpīḍa who had entered within, her hand fell upon her heart.
That very sprout-like hand, that very arm, became a pretext for covering her breasts;
it was joy itself that shed the water of tears.
The pollen from the flowers of her swaying ear-ornaments served as a pretext;
bashfulness itself did not permit her to speak.
The swarm of bees attracted by the fragrance of her lotus-face took on the role of doorkeepers;
the very sensation of pain from the first strike of Love’s arrow produced a whistling sound (*sītkāra*),
while the wound from the thorns of the flower-clusters in the garden became a common occurrence.
A trembling alone caused her palm to shake;
the warding off of the female doorkeeper who had come to announce him became a mere pretext.
And at that moment, as Kādambarī entered, there seemed to be a second god of love even for the God of Love himself.
Candrāpīḍa’s heart entered into her;
for indeed, he regarded the brilliance of her jeweled ornaments as a disappearance,
and he considered his entry into her heart to be her formal acceptance.
He considered even the conversation [with her] to be an ornament; he imagined even the captivation of all his senses to be a favor;
and he conceived even the contact with the radiance of her body to be the bliss of a union in love.
Kādambarī, as if with great difficulty, having taken only a few steps, embraced Mahāśvetā around the neck with deep affection, her longing born from the long duration of their separation;
and Mahāśvetā, having likewise embraced her very firmly, said to her: “Friend Kādambarī!”

In the land of Bhārata, there was a king named Tārāpīḍa, who protected his subjects from the pain caused by the pricks of the hooves of many excellent horses, having established the four-fold seal [of justice]; his son,

named Candrāpīḍa— who bore the burden of the entire earth resting upon the stone-pillars of his own arms, who was a friend to the whole world— having arrived at this region in the course of his conquest of the quarters.

And from the moment he was first seen, this man has become by nature my friend without cause; for, having captivated my mental disposition with his exceptionally noble and naturally upright virtues, he dwells within it—having overcome even that hardness which results from the abandonment of all attachments. Indeed, rare is the refined person who, being under the sway of courtesy, is a sincere-hearted friend without motive; for upon merely seeing him, you too, just as I have, will recognize his skill in creation.
The unrivaled beauty of her form,
the steadfastness of Fortune’s residence,
and the happiness of the Earth having a virtuous lord.
He perceived the superiority of the mortal world over the celestial realm,
the fruitfulness of human eyes,
and the convergence of all the arts in a single place.
"You shall know the sovereign power of good fortune and the refined elegance of men; therefore, this man has been brought here by force.
And I have described him to my dear friend in many ways as being most beneficial."
Casting aside shame on the grounds that he was a person never seen before, abandoning diffidence because he had not yet become acquainted with him,
and discarding suspicion because his character was unknown;
"When she said, 'Just as you have behaved toward me, so should you behave here;
this is your friend, your kinsman, and your attendant,' Candrāpīḍa made his salutation."

And as he then offered his salutation, a cluster of drops of tears of joy fell from the eyes of Kādambarī as she glanced sideways at him— drops that seemed like a spreading spray of sweat-water from the pupils of her exceedingly long eyes as they reached the corners of her gaze.
As she set out in haste, the moonlight of her smile, white as plaster, spread forth like dust.

[he approached] Indrāyudha’s saddle-cloth, which was partially drawn aside to one side.

Straightening and smoothing out his mane— which had fallen slightly on one side and slightly on the other— and casting aside the saffron-brown tuft of hair between his eyes that obstructed his vision, he placed his hooves firmly upon the ground and, resting the weight of his body against the wooden bars of the stable, spoke with playful languor and curiosity: "Keyūraka!"
Tell me, what news has occurred in the Gandharva king’s palace since my departure? With what occupation did the Gandharva princess pass the day? And what did Mahāśvetā do?
What did Madalekhā say?
What were the conversations with the attendants? And what was your own occupation?
"Was there any conversation concerning us?
Keyūraka replied, "My Lord, listen:
when you had departed, the maiden’s inner apartments—making, as it were, a tumultuous din like the sound of drums for the departure of a thousand hearts with the tinkling of their many anklets—"
Queen Kādambarī, accompanied by her attendants, ascended the roof-terrace of the palace and gazed upon the path of the King’s departure, which was grey with the streaks of dust raised by his horses.
When the King had vanished from sight,
she rested her face upon the shoulder of Madalekhā and, out of affection, seemed to drench him with showers of glances as white as the ocean of milk.
Under the pretext of being a parasol against the heat, she remained there for a very long time, warding off the touch of the sun’s rays out of jealousy toward the moon.

Then, having somehow descended from there with evident weariness and stayed for a moment in the pavilion of the assembly hall, she rose and, as if fearing a stumble, had the offering flowers presented to her by the humming bees.
With bracelets slipping down her neck as if forming a collar, their white rays reflecting from her nails that were bright as streams of water, she— distressed by the cries of the palace peacocks—

reached that very pleasure-mountain where the Prince had stayed; there, at every step, she grasped with her hand the flower-white sprouts of the house-creepers while her mind clung to the multitude of the Prince’s virtues.

Approaching him, he saw him staying there in a vine-arbor where green creepers were being sprinkled by water flowing from a makara-shaped spout carved from emerald stone; he saw him standing upon a dappled stone surface,
having bathed in that place where the rocky ground was thick with swarms of bees clinging to the fragrance of scented bathing waters.
Here, on the bank of a mountain stream amidst sands of flower-pollen—[on the slope of the Blue Mountain of sand and mud]—the Lord Śūlapāṇi was worshipped;
here, upon a crystal stone slab whose luster put the moon to shame, we feasted; and here, upon a couch of stone slabs from the Pearl Mountain, marked with the imprint of sandalwood paste.
As the attendants repeatedly announced, "He has fallen asleep," she spent the day observing the very signs of the King's presence.
At the close of day, with great effort on Mahāśvetā’s part, she somehow took her meal in that very chamber of crystal stone slabs, though it was against her will.
When the Blessed Sun had set and the moon had risen,

she remained there for some time; her body moistened as if made of moonstone at the rising of the moon, she placed her hands upon her cheeks as if in fear of entering the lunar orb, and pondered something within herself.

With her eyes half-closed, she remained for a moment and then rose; with great effort, as if lifting heavy ornaments—the reflections of the moon fallen upon her spotless nails—she went to the bedchamber, taking steps that were skillfully slow and graceful out of coquetry. There, she cast her slender body upon the couch.

From that time forth, writhing in powerful headaches and overwhelmed by a terrible fever characterized by a burning sensation, she— afflicted by some mental anguish (*ādhi*) or physical illness (*vyādhi*)— spent the night in extreme misery with her eyes unblinking, like auspicious lamps, lilies,
and *cakravāka* birds.
And having summoned me, she instructed me reproachfully to obtain news of the King’s condition.
Upon hearing this, Candrāpīḍa, desiring to depart and his mind filled with wonder at the events that had transpired, went forth from the palace saying, "Horse! Horse!"
Having mounted a horse with its saddle already fastened, which was brought by his attendants and whose trappings were swift,
and having had Patralekhā mount behind him,
he left Vaiśampāyana at the camp.
Having dismissed his entire retinue and being followed by Keyūraka, who was mounted upon a horse, he proceeded to Hemakūṭa.

Upon reaching the gate of Kādambarī’s palace, he dismounted from his horse. Having dismounted and handed over his steed to the doorkeeper, he entered while Kādambarī, eager for her first sight of him, looked out.
Followed by Patralekhā, he entered and asked a certain eunuch who came toward him, "Where does the lady Kādambarī stay? To which the eunuch,
having made his salutation, replied, "O King..."

When Keyūraka had thus informed him that [the prince] was seated within a crystal summer-house situated on the bank of a lotus-pond at the foot of the Pleasure-Mountain, where peacocks were dancing, he proceeded through the middle of the pleasure-grove along the path being pointed out by Keyūraka,
having traveled a short distance.
He beheld a day whose solar rays were turned into young grass and which was made green by the luster of groves of plantain trees, verdant like emeralds;
and in their midst, he saw a snow-palace covered by the dense leaves of lotus ponds.
And from it emerged a youth, seemingly clothed in the waters of the Acchoda lake under the guise of moist garments.
His limbs were whitened by ornaments of lotus-fiber bracelets held in his vine-like arms;

his face-lotuses bore forehead-marks of sandalwood paste applied like painted seals of good fortune, while the inner petals of *ketakī* flowers, pale white and worn as earrings upon one ear, mocked the beauty of ivory ear-ornaments.

He bore cheeks upon which special marks of sandalwood paste had been applied, appearing even by day like reflections of the moon lingering there out of a longing for their touch; he wore ear-ornaments fashioned from clusters of *śaivala* moss that had stolen away the entire beauty of the *śirīṣa* flower;
and he was adorned with circular wreaths of *bakula* blossoms, which were drenched in camphor powder and mingled with drops of sandalwood juice.
Upon her breasts— like clusters of blue water-lilies and delicate bracelets— she had placed a covering of lotus leaves;
these were rendered pale by the constant application of sandalwood paste, appearing as if they were the very rays of the moon, reddened by the heat of her fever and softened by her resentment.
He bore chowries made of lotus fibers with handles fashioned from lotus stalks revealed by the pressure of his hands;
he was shielded from the heat by parasols formed of upturned lotuses, water-lilies, blue lilies, tender shoots, plantain leaves, lotus petals, and clusters of blossoms;
and he appeared like a host of water-deities.
Like a gathering at the abode of Varuṇa,
like an assembly of autumns,
like a social circle formed by lakes;
He beheld Kādambarī’s retinue, who were almost entirely female attendants, skilled in providing cooling remedies and devoted to the service of her body;
and as he was being saluted by them, they retreated with haste, as if fearing the crushing of their feet or the burning heat of his toe-nails, while clearing a path for him.
[The gardens] had platforms made of sandalwood paste, with small bells fashioned from lotus buds;
they possessed chowries made of clusters of blossoming *sindhuvāra* flowers, and hanging necklaces of thick jasmine buds;

they were adorned with garlands of *lavaṅga* sprouts and sandalwood, and featured banners of swaying water-lily wreaths, [guarded] by women holding lotus-stalk staves in their hands and wearing beautiful flower ornaments, appearing like personified embodiments of the Goddess of Spring.
Having entered through the gateway of plantain arches guarded by female door-keepers as if they were [the goddesses] Prakṛtis, he cast his gaze in every direction and beheld:
in some places, forest-borders fashioned from *tāla* sprouts planted on both banks and buried within.

House-rivers were flowing with sandalwood juice, their banks garlanded with the pollen-dust of *kumuda* lotuses; in some places, red chowries made of *nicula* flower-clusters were suspended beneath canopies moistened with water over floors inlaid with vermilion, where carpets were being spread,
and in other places, walls whose beautiful surfaces could only be inferred by touch were being sprinkled with the essence of *elā*.
In some places, there were crystal palaces with grounds whose delightful locations could be inferred by touch;

in others, there were mica palaces where one was being led up to the peaks of lotus-stalk water-chambers— covered in green turf made from the fibers of *śirīṣa* blossoms— and greyed by the pollen of *kadamba* flowers falling from the showers.
...clusters of mechanical peacocks that were greyish;
in some places, leaf-huts whose interiors were being covered by rose-apple sprouts moistened with the juice of mango trees;
and in other places, golden lotus-pools being agitated by herds of artificial young elephants engaged in play.

In some places, there were water-wheel contrivances (*ghaṭī-yantraka*) made of lotus leaves, being wound with ropes of blue-lotus garlands; these wheels had buckets (*droṇikā*) fashioned from thick lotus-stalk stems, their rims bound with gold and lime-mud, and their handles fashioned from golden *ketaka* flowers, while the water-channels (*jala-droṇikā*) were formed by the petals themselves.
In some places, there were moving illusory clouds, appearing as rows of crystal cranes with rainbows drawn by the streams of water they emitted;
in other places,
pearl necklaces were being cooled in pools of liquid yellow sandalwood, whose ripples were jagged with white jasmine buds on trees and where pale barley sprouts grew along the edges.

In some places, there were mechanical trees emitting a cloudy mist from incessant, thick drops of water, like small fountains fashioned from crushed pearls; in other places, there were rows of mechanical birds made of leaves, whirling about and bringing down frost through sprays discharged by the flapping of their wings;
and in yet other places, there were [mechanical lotuses] being struck by the exceedingly sharp sound of the tinkling of bees acting as tiny bells.

In some places, flower-wreath swings were being vigorously shaken; in others, golden jars with their mouths covered by lotus petals—whose stalks had emerged from within and risen high—were being brought inside;
in some places, beautiful umbrella-like canopies made of clusters of flowers, with handles fashioned from the inner stems of plantain trees, were being fastened;
and in other places, silken garments made of lotus fibers were being perfumed with the juice of camphor shoots crushed by hand.

In some places he observed the attendants moistening with the juice of *lavalī* fruit the *karmapūra* clusters of the *tṛṇaśūnya* plant; in other places, fanning with lotus-leaf fans the cold medicinal juices contained in vessels of *ulapa* reed; and observing other such activities of the servants engaged in preparing various cooling remedies, both those already completed and those currently being performed.
It was the central part of a palace of snow, as it were the very heart of the Himalayas; like a pleasure-pavilion for Varuṇa for his aquatic sports;
like a land not frequented by any of the digits of the moon;
and like the ancestral home of all the deities of the sandalwood forests.
It was like the source of all moonstones,
the dwelling place of all nights in the month of Māgha, and the meeting hall for all rainy seasons.
It was like a hook for removing the heat of summer from all rivers,
a dwelling for dispelling the scorching of the submarine fire from all oceans,
and a place of remedy for the burning of lightning-fire for all clouds.

For the night-lotuses themselves, who endure days difficult to pass due to their separation from the moon; for the god of love, it was like a sacrificial field for the fire of Śiva; and for the forest deities, it was like a dwelling place—even the rays of the sun, though driven away on all sides by thousands of streams from water-machines, seemed to have retreated out of fear of its extreme coldness.
It was shielded even by fires that bore clusters of *kadamba* filaments and seemed as if covered in bristling hair;
it was surrounded even by groves of plantain trees whose leaves were stirred by the wind, as if trembling from the chill of cold;
and it was made resonant even by bees, who, intoxicated by the fragrance of the flowers, seemed to have their teeth chattering like lutes.
He reached [the place], which was resplendent with creepers dense with swarms of bees, appearing as if they had donned dark blue mantles;

and there, being gradually smeared on the inside and outside by an exceedingly thick, cool touch— as if by a mass of cooling unguent— he perceived his own mind to be made of moonlight and his senses to be made of white water-lilies.
He perceived his limbs as consisting of moonlight, his intellect as consisting of lotus stalks,
and the rays of the sun as consisting of necklaces— or rather, as consisting of frost.
The sunlight was made of sandalwood,
the breeze was made of camphor, and the season was made of spring.
The three worlds consist of frost;
and in one part of such a place, she saw her, surrounded by a circle of female friends,
like the divine Gaṅgā— herself the retinue of all rivers— dwelling within a cave of the Himavat mountains, situated upon a mountain that serves as her home.
She lay upon a bed of flowers beneath a bower of lotus stalks, which was surrounded by a halo of camphor-juice flowing in circular ripples upon the surface of the earth;
she seemed bound by her own jealousy with fetters of lotus-fiber consisting of necklaces, armlets, bracelets, girdles, and anklets, as if seized by the God of Love,
and touched on the forehead— white as sandalwood— with the moon.
In her eyes, which were shedding streams of tears, she was as if kissed by the wind;
in her mouth, where the breath of sighing was increasing, she was as if bitten by the breeze;
and upon her limbs, heated by the fever of passion, she was as if sat upon by the fire of love.
As if seized by the heart by Kandarpa, who was inflamed by the fever of love;
as if embraced by water upon her perspiring body, O Jaladeva;
and as if her good fortune were being plundered on all sides even by the gods.
Her limbs had approached a state of near-union with her most beloved heart, causing her to become weak;
she bore a horripilation as pale as dried sandalwood paste, which seemed like a mass of pearls clinging to her from the incessant touch of her necklace.
And her cheeks, sprinkled with drops of perspiration, were being comforted, as it were, by the bees in her ear-ornaments who fanned them with the breeze of their wings.

She wore a *karpūra- ketakī* bud as an earring on her ear, serving as a conduit for the excessive flow of tears that issued from the corners of her eyes— tears which seemed to scorch her ears like a forest fire ignited by the humming of bees amidst the flowers of her ear-ornament.
Her jar-like breasts were being released from the silken garment, which, trembling with long-drawn sighs, appeared to flee in fear of the heat, as if it were the very luster of her body.

With her pair of jar-like breasts reflecting the falling, swaying fly-whisks— [in some versions, "the falling, powerful fly-whisk"]— she seemed to be warding off with her palm a wing outstretched in eagerness to approach her beloved;
again and again, she embraced a statue carved from ice with her vine-like arm.
Now and then she would press a camphor statuette against the surface of her cheek, and now and then she would stroke the reflection of the sandalwood paste upon her lotus-foot;
even with her own face reflected in her breasts, she seemed to turn and gaze at it as if out of curiosity.
Her cheeks were being kissed, as it were with longing, even by the sprouts of her ear-ornaments resting upon them like sprouts of her own reflection;

she was being embraced by her pearl necklaces, which, though composed of detached pearls, seemed to extend their hands out of subjection to Love; and she held to her breast a jeweled mirror—a moon that was a pledge of life, as if saying, "Do not rise today," or rather, "You must console me today"—as if it were the very touch of life itself.

She was making the moon appear as if it were the very moment of the touch of life, like a female elephant extending her trunk toward a scent-elephant from the pleasure grove that had approached her face-to-face.
She was like a departing vessel whose favorable wind and deer have not yet arrived;
she was like an altar for the consecration of Love, her sides embraced by the jar-like breasts white with sandalwood paste and covered with lotuses;
she was like a celestial lotus-pond, the base of her thighs as tender as lotus stalks visible against the clear expanse of the sky.
She was more beautiful than the tip of the string fixed upon the bow of the God of Love, like a streak of the flower-bowed god’s own bow;
she was like the deity of the spring month, dispelling the cold;
and she was like a female bee, restless in her pursuit of flowers.

She beheld Kādambarī, who was anointed with sandalwood paste, possessed a passion for the bodiless god (Kāma), was as lovely as a lotus stalk— the very mother of love— and had requested the touch of cool frost.
Then, as each arrived according to her sight, she, with pupils trembling, [beheld] the attendants announcing the arrival of Candrāpīḍa.

"How far away is she, and where? he asked, casting his eyes toward her while the syllables of her name were inscribed [in his mind]. And seeing him approaching directly from afar with eyes whose whiteness was increasing, the woman of noble form—*varārohā*—beheld him.
The Nine Planets, their limbs struggling as they were held by the elephant-like pillar of her thighs, were being raised up—
as if by swarms of buzzing bees drawn to the fragrance of her flower-bed— while she was being covered by them;
her upper garment fell away in her agitation.
Desiring to place the rays of her necklace upon her breast with her upper garment, she seemed to beg for support from her own reflection by resting the palm of her left hand upon the jeweled floor;
and with her right hand— exhausted by the toil of binding her disheveled mass of hair and dripping with perspiration— she seemed to sprinkle herself with water as she offered herself up.
As if being squeezed by the god of love through the line of hair that rippled with the three folds of her waist— trembling as she moved and shimmering like waves—
and as if infused with the sandalwood paste from the forehead-mark that had entered within, she seemed to extract all the essences [of passion].
With her eyes— her two eyes— flowing with cool tears of joy,

her cheek-surface greyed by the pollen from her ear-ornament which had shifted due to the stream of teardrops of bliss, she bent her face slightly downward as if out of longing for the entry of her beloved’s image; at that moment, she was being drawn away by a long gaze whose pupils were concentrated on the corner of his eye, as if fixed upon his face.
She rose from her bed of flowers.

Candrāpīḍa, however, having approached, bowed to her with the same humility as before, preceded by a prostration to Mahāśvetā. When she had returned his bow and sat down once more upon that very same bed of flowers, he too sat down.
Having pushed aside with her foot a golden throne that had been brought forward by the female attendants— a throne whose legs were inlaid with radiant jewels— she sat down upon the bare ground.
Then Keyūraka said, "O Queen!"
"This is Patralekhā by name, the bearer of the betel casket and the object of Prince Candrāpīḍa’s favor," she said, and showed her Patralekhā.
Then, having seen her, Kādambarī thought, "Oh! What partiality the Creator shows toward mortal women!"

When she had offered her salutation, I said respectfully, "Come, come," and seated her near me while she was watched with curiosity by my attendants; from the very moment I saw her, an excess of affection arose within me, and I repeatedly touched her with my sprout-like hand in a supportive manner.

Candrāpīḍa, however, having immediately performed all the customary rites of welcome, beheld the daughter of Citraratha in that state and thought: "My heart is indeed excessively callous, for even now it does not believe; well then, I shall ask her with skillful words.
[Addressing her openly, he said: "O Queen!"

"I know, daughter, that this disease—intense with incessant torment—has arisen taking pleasure in sensual desires as its cause. Truly, it does not afflict you as much as it afflicts me. I desire to restore your ladyship to health, even by the sacrifice of my own body."

As I look upon you, trembling and fallen under the torment of the flower-arrowed god, my heart seems to fall with you. O you who are without ornaments, whose slender arms are like the creepers of the deity Anaṅga, and who possess eyes filled with intense heat, you bear the likeness of a land-lotus with its red lotuses.

While you are suffering, and while even your attendants are constantly shedding falling teardrops, the state of being bereft of ornaments persists. Take for yourself the auspicious decorations worthy of a *svayaṃvara*; for a fresh creeper shines when accompanied by flowers and bees. Furthermore, [the text continues]: "...constantly... [and so forth].
Even the attendants remain with a constant falling of teardrops;
take up the state of being adorned with pearls—
for a creeper shines when hidden by flowers and bees.

Then Kādambarī, though naturally innocent due to her youth, grasped with her mind that meaning— which had been indicated by his entire demeanor and unspoken discourse— as if through an intellect instructed by the God of Love; yet,
unable to conceive of such a realm for her desires and maintaining her modesty, she remained silent.
At that very moment, her face— darkened by the swarm of bees attracted to the fragrance of her smile— cast a smile as if to look upon it;
then Madalekhā replied, “O Prince, O delicate one,
what shall I say?”
This is indeed a terrible and unspeakable anguish.
Moreover, for one so delicate and endowed with the nature of a maiden, what is there that would not cause her distress?
For instance, even a cool sprout acts like a fire to a lotus plant.
"Even the moonlight acts like the heat of the sun;
do you not see that she experiences distress in her mind even from the breeze of a leaf-fan?
Only her fortitude is the cause that sustains her life."

Kādambarī, however, with her heart, gave him that very reply which had been spoken by Madalekhā. Candrāpīḍa, too, his mind mounted upon the swing of doubt because the matter could be interpreted in either way, spent a long time with Mahāśvetā in conversations skillful at increasing their affection— conversations whose essence was like the flow of honey.
Having remained there for some time and having likewise freed himself with great effort, he departed from Kādambarī’s palace to go to his military camp.
As he was about to mount his horse after departing, Keyūraka approached from behind and said: “O Lord!”

Madalekhā reports: "Queen Kādambarī, having conceived an affection for Patralekhā at their first meeting, wishes her to return; she will depart later. Having heard this, "Your Majesty is the authority," said Candrāpīḍa upon hearing it, "Keyūraka!"
"Blessed and enviable is Patralekhā, whom Your Majesty thus favors;
rare indeed is the favor of the Queen—let her be admitted. Having spoken thus, he returned once more to the royal camp. (5) [He approached; he went.]
As he was entering, he saw a well-known torch-bearer approaching from his father's presence;
and having halted his horse, with eyes wide with joy, he asked him from afar:
"My good man, is my father well, together with all his attendants?"
"And so too my mother, along with all the ladies of the inner apartments.
Then, having approached and offered his salutations, he said, "Your Majesty,
as you command," and presented two letters.

The prince, however, placing it upon his head and removing it himself, read it aloud in succession: "Hail! From Ujjayinī, the Great King of Kings, the supreme devotee of Maheśvara, the divine Tārāpīḍa—whose lotus-feet are made into crest-jewels by the crowns of all noblemen—salutes Candrāpīḍa, the abode of all prosperity, and gladdens him by kissing his head, which is touched by the circle of rays from his rising and beautiful crest-jewel."
The subjects are well-being;
however, how much time has passed since you were last seen— [you who are] most excellent—
and our hearts are intensely longing [for you], even more so when accompanied by the Queen.

And the queen, along with the women of the inner apartments, had been reduced to a state of despondency; therefore, the cessation of the reading of the letter itself was to be brought about as the occasion for the departure [of the prince]. (In some versions, the reading "by the auspicious one" is additionally found.)
The second letter sent by Śukanāsa also read out this very same matter in its entirety.
At that very moment, Vaiśampāyana also approached and presented two other letters of his own, which were identical in meaning to those.
Then, saying, "As my father commands," he mounted his horse and, in that very manner, had the drum of departure sounded.

And he gave instructions to Meghanāda, the son of Balāhaka, who was standing nearby, surrounded by a great troop of cavalry, and who held the office of commander-in-chief: "Keyūraka will certainly come this far with Patralekhā and those others."

Having bowed, you must inform Queen Kādambarī through his mouth: "Indeed, this person is one whom the three worlds ought to despise—devoid of affection and lacking in familiarity. For those whose affections are so difficult to grasp, being inconsistent even at unexpected moments, do not take account of groundless kindness.
By departing in this manner, I have reduced my own affection to the state of a deceptive snare."
Devotion has been reduced to a proficiency in feigning false affectation; the surrender of one’s self has been cast into a deceitfulness sweetened by mere formalities;
and a discrepancy between speech and mind has been made manifest.

Let the matter of the self be set aside for now; even the Goddess, who is worthy of divine favor, has been brought to a state of reproach by her misplaced confidence. For when the nectar-like showers of the great ones' favor fall upon an unworthy ground, they produce later a sense of embarrassment, being rendered futile.

Indeed, my heart is not burdened by such a weight of intense shame toward the Queen as it is toward Mahāśvetā. Surely the Queen will repeatedly reproach her for falsely imputing qualities to me that I do not possess, and for her misplaced partiality. So, what shall I do?

The command of a superior is more weighty; for it prevails even over a mere god. Yet, with a heart devoted to dwelling on Hemakūṭa, I have written this bond of servitude to the Queen for a thousand future births. It has not been surrendered to this forest-dweller, just as a toll-collector does not surrender his dues to a forest bandit.
It was not placed in the hands of the Queen, as if by a forest-dwelling guard; yet, by the grace of the Queen, I am to go.

In every way, I have gone to Ujjayinī at my father’s command. Incidentally, while discussing the talk of wicked people, this outcaste Candrāpīḍa must indeed be remembered. (Note: In some versions, the phrase "talk of wicked people" is absent. 6. In some places, the word "outcaste" (*caṇḍāla*) does not appear.

Do not think that Candrāpīḍa will remain here merely experiencing the joy of worshipping the lotus-feet of the Goddess again while alive, [but rather] he shall remain until he has experienced those lotus-feet;
and Mahāśvetā’s feet must be worshipped by him with his head as a seventh prostration.
And Madalekhā must be offered a firm embrace around the neck preceded by a salutation;
Tamālikā, moreover, must be closely embraced.
On my behalf, every member of Kādambary’s retinue should be inquired after regarding their welfare.

"And with palms joined in reverence, the Blessed One is to be addressed as 'Hemakūṭa,'" he said. Having thus instructed him, and having told him, "Even by a friend, one should proceed slowly and without causing distress to those who assist," he appointed Vaiśampāyana to the burden of the camp.

He himself, mounted upon a horse of such a kind, was followed by a cavalry force consisting mostly of young horses, which— shaking Mount Kailāsa with the playful neighing born of the joy of their gallop, tearing up the earth with the frantic dancing of their hooves, and sweeping away groves of lovely spear-like grass— was following that very messenger who remained attached to his saddle-pediment, even though [the king] was already empty at heart due to his recent separation from Kādambarī.
With his heart set on news of Ujjayinī, he set out, inquiring after the road to Ujjayinī. By degrees, he reached a region abounding in trees with massive trunks,
where groves of trees were encircled by circles of *mālinī* creeper arbors.

[The path] was made crooked by the avoidance of trees felled by the lord of elephants, where the spots of slaughter of heroic men were revealed by heaps of grass, leaves, and wood-pieces thrown down by people,
and where the wilderness was difficult to traverse due to great trees uprooted from the ground.

[The river] was [adorned] with heaps of *āmalaka* fruits abandoned by thirsty travelers who had stripped away their leaves; its banks were sprinkled with the pollen from the blossoming clusters of *karañja* and *kapikacchū*; it bore the banners of rags tied to the trees on its banks like those of a bandit; and it resounded with the shaking of weary travelers resting upon dry leaf-mats made of bricks and twigs, inferred by their presence there.

By those ancient wilderness wells, whose vicinity was marked by sprouts grey with the dust of feet that had been crushed [therein], and whose waters were cool, muddy, discolored, and tasteless due to being made foul-smelling by the accumulation of fallen leaves; and which, because water was so difficult to obtain, indicated their existence only by the signs of leaf-cups tied in knots upon creepers and the presence of grass-hoppers and parched grain; and thus, they were situated in regions that could not even be mentioned.

Its intervals were made uneven by dried mountain streams whose banks were grey with the pollen from groves of *sinduvāra* trees dripping honey-drops, whose sandy beds were overgrown with masses of *kuñjaka* creepers, and which contained only small amounts of turbid water found in wells dug by travelers in the sand.
Having wandered through the forest for the day along a deserted village path— dense with thickets inferred by the cries of cocks,
dogs, and jackals— when the orb of the sun had set and the day was reddened by the spreading glow of the twilight’s crimson hue.

[The forest was] filled with *kadamba*, *śālmalī*, and *palāśa* trees that had been stripped of their branches, their single remaining sprouts at the tips mimicking royal parasols; and it was further composed of thickets of ripe bamboo,
tawny as yellow orpiment, entwined with the knotted roots and massive trunks of trees whose upward-growing shoots had become thick and stunted.

In a region of the Vajra district where the forest areas were thinned out by woodland fields consisting mostly of *priyaṅgu* plants— fields that were covered with fences made of branches and leaves, filled with grass-dummies placed there out of fear of deer, and rendered pale by their ripening and laden with fruit.
Above a red sandalwood tree that had long since grown deep, yet appeared fresh from afar, was tied [a banner] with lac-resins resembling lumps of fresh flesh,
and with red flags as crimson as tongues of fresh blood, moistened by the juice of red sandalwood as red as fresh blood.

Its staff was adorned with a black yak-tail plume possessing the luster of a mass of hair, fashioned as if from the limbs of living beings freshly slaughtered; it was inlaid with crescent-shaped fragments of pearls strung together with cowries;
and its top shone as if the moon had descended there, brought down by the Sun who had himself alighted to protect his own son, the buffalo.

From afar, he beheld a great red banner that seemed to scrape the very surface of the sky with a golden trident adorned with a beautiful yak-tail chowrie fashioned from a lion’s mane, and which was made terrifying by the jangling sound of iron chains hanging from its swaying prongs; it appeared as if it were surveying here and there a path for the sacrifice of wayfarers for some distance.
Having traveled some distance toward it,
he beheld [the city] enclosed by a forest-elephant’s ivory gate as white as a cluster of *ketakī* flower spikes,
and adorned with a copper archway surrounded by rows of fresh red chowries; it bore a garland of circular iron mirrors that was as terrifying as a garland of Śabara heads with their tawny hair.

And [he saw] a stone slab altar occupied by a red iron buffalo, which stood facing forward with its forefeet planted like clumps of red sandalwood; its eyes were blood-red, licked by female jackals greedy for drops of blood, as if it were being struck by the palm of Yama’s hand, which was as crimson as applied red sandalwood.

In some places it was with red lotuses, like the eyes of forest buffaloes struck down by Śabaras; in some places with buds of *agasti* flowers, like the claws of lions; and in some places with buds of *kiṃśuka* flowers, like the blood-stained talons of tigers.
The sacrificial slaughter was strewn with flowers of accumulated merit;

elsewhere, it appeared as if sprouted by the curved tips of the horns of crooked deer, as if budding with hundreds of fresh tongues and frothing mouths, as if flowering with thousands of blood-red eyes, and as if bearing fruit in the form of circles of severed heads. Flocks of red cocks were nestled without interval among the branches.
The city was adorned with red *śoka* trees whose clusters of blossoms appeared as if bitten out of season due to the fear of dogs and the fear of flocks of cocks;
it offered up sacrifices of severed heads and fruit by *tāla* trees that seemed like *vetālas* arrived out of a thirst to drink the blood of the sacrificial offerings;

and it was surrounded on all sides by groves of plantains trembling as if with the fever of apprehension, by thickets of *śrīphala* trees agitated by fear, and by date-palm forests with their fronds bristling upward as if their hair stood on end from terror.

Its outskirts were not deserted by playful lion cubs— spoiled by their upbringing under Ambikā— who were scattering pearls fallen from the temples of forest elephants they had torn apart; these pearls, red with blood, were being greedily seized and then released by charming jungle cocks, while the cubs themselves were eager for the rows of fresh, blood-red pearls.

With the sun, reddened by its setting, reflected as if fallen into a swoon born of the sight of so much [blood], the streams of blood-water made it even more crimson; with hanging lamp-smoke acting as red silk banners, with rows of fire-tufted necklaces suspended like garlands,
and bearing heavy bells whitened by heaps of flour-paste.
