and by the lac-dye stains falling upon the pedestal of the inner image— stains that resembled all the lives of sacrificial animals seeking refuge, appearing as if they were masses of lac or cloths of lac-dye.
Her feet were never parted from foot-cloths dyed with lac juice;

and because of the luster of her life-slaying weapons— such as axes, spears, and battle-axes— their reflections of fallen black yak-tail fans appeared like masses of hair clinging to severed heads, creating a dense darkness.

She appeared like a dweller of the underworld (pātāla), as if residing in a subterranean cave, adorned with garlands of *bilva* leaves that were fashioned from sprouts and throbbing fruit-slices inlaid with red sandalwood, resembling a necklace of severed children’s heads.
Adorned with ornaments,
[her body] copper-red with blood,
and with worship performed using clusters of *kadamba* blossoms, she was made to tremble with intense emotion by the resonant beating of drums for the animal sacrifice.

She bore a cruelness with her limbs that were bristling with horripilation; her forehead was covered by a beautiful band of refined gold and marked with a dot of vermilion paste applied by a Śabara maiden;
the surface of her cheeks was turning crimson from the radiance of a pomegranate-stone earring, and the hollow of her lower lip was reddened by blood-stained betel.

With a face whose tawny eyes were curved by a frown and whose gaze was blood-red, and with a body clad in a silk garment as pale-red as safflower, she bore the graceful allure of Mahākālī dressed for a tryst.

With the flickering garlands of inner-chamber lamps, reddened by the smoke of blended blue *guggulu* incense— resembling fingers with their tips formed into a circle— and appearing crimson as if stained by drops of the blood of the demon Mahiṣa, she seemed to be threatening a wild buffalo that had offended her by scratching its shoulder-pads against the staff of her trident.
She was being worshipped by goats with long, hanging beards as if they were observers of vows;
by mice with quivering lips as if they were intent on silent recitation (*japa*);

by deer with their bodies covered in black antelope skins as if they were lying down for rest; and even by black cobras with the rays of the red gems on their heads blazing forth, appearing as if they held jeweled lamps upon their heads.
She was being praised, as it were, by a flock of harsh-cawing crows chirping from every side;

and she was made to look like a lattice-window by the very thick networks of veins upon her, which— resembling swarms of lizards, chameleons, and *godhālikā* or *godhāragodhikā* lizards— had climbed up as if suspecting them to be scorched tree-stumps.
His entire body was mottled with spots from boils that resembled the marks of ill fortune eradicated [by his asceticism];
he wore a crest-lock fixed as an ear-ornament like a rosary of *rudrākṣa* beads;
and he bore a swelling on his forehead, darkened by falling at the feet of Ambikā.
Kuvādidatta,

whose one eye was opened by the application of magical ointment (*siddhāñjana*), would daily apply smooth wooden rods as ointment to his other eye at the three times of day; he also daily undertook the remedy for his protruding teeth by means of sweating them with bitter *alābu* gourds.
By having somehow dealt a blow with a stone at an improper place; by having his addiction to massage somehow calmed by a single dry arm;
by having his cataracts increased through the incessant application of pungent medicinal wicks;
and by possessing boar’s tusks secured for the purpose of splitting stones.
He was carrying a collection of medicinal ointments and collyria prepared from *iṅgudī* wood;
his left hand was contracted with its veins stitched together by a needle;
and his big toe was wounded and scarred by the friction of a silken garment used as a covering.
He was afflicted by an untimely fever brought on by improperly prepared elixirs;

though he had reached old age, he was tormented by his difficult mountain fortress due to his pursuit of the boon of sovereignty over the Dakṣiṇāpatha; and he placed his hopes for prosperity upon a sectarian mark applied at the bidding of ill-trained ascetics.
Carrying conch shells soiled by ink made from the juice of green leaves and charcoal;
bearing a scroll inscribed with hymns to difficult fortresses;
and holding a small book containing fraudulent treatises on spells and mechanical devices, with characters written in smoke-red lac.
[This is] the *Jīrṇapāśupatopadeśa*, written according to the opinion of Mahākāla,
[a work] afflicted by the doctrine of manifesting hidden treasures (*nidhi*) and possessed by the wind of the doctrine of alchemy (*dhātuvāda*).
By the demon of entering the cave of the ascendant,
by the delusion of the desire for union with a yakṣa maiden that has arisen,
and by the accumulation of the practice of spells for invisibility— <1> <1...by the collection of spells for invisibility>.

He was one who possessed direct knowledge of thousands of wondrous reports from Śrīparvata; he was one whose ears were flattened by the slapping of palms by those possessed by *piśāca* spirits, who had been driven away by the repeated striking of consecrated mustard seeds, yet who remained unfit even for his ears and nostrils.
It was not abandoned because of the pride of being a devotee of Śiva, but rather avoided by travelers who were distressed by the playing of lutes made from gourds that were poorly grasped.
During the day itself, he sang with a voice imitating the buzzing of a mosquito, his hair standing on end; he was a dancer of a hymn of devotion to the Bhāgīrathī composed in his own native dialect,
and because he had observed the vow of celibacy toward horses, he had repeatedly employed a woman-subjugating powder upon elderly female ascetics who had come from other lands and stayed there.

Sometimes, due to extreme irritability, he would violently mock even the goddess Caṇḍikā with contortions of his face, provoked by anger arising from the fall of a poorly placed *aṣṭapuṣpikā* die; sometimes, while being restrained, his back was broken by falling in a multi-armed wrestling match initiated by a traveler enraged by the sound of his garment; and sometimes, with his arms constantly raised and his neck and brow knitted by the shaking of his head, he appeared blood-red.

Sometimes, with his neck bent and the skull of his head split open after falling face-down while stumbling as he ran in pursuit out of anger at a fleeing boy who had committed an offense; sometimes, his mind inflamed by envy toward the respect shown to newly arrived ascetics from other regions by the people of the countryside;
and acting as he pleased due to a lack of refinement.
Because of his lameness, he moved very slowly; because of his deafness, he communicated through gestures;
because of his night-blindness, he wandered about during the day.
Due to his pot-belliedness, he was a great consumer;
his nostrils had been pierced by the scratches of monkeys' claws many times in their anger as they tried to shake down fruit;
and his body had been mangled by the stings of thousands of bees that had swarmed around him while he gathered flowers. <1> <1.Asārīkṛta...> (rendered worthless...)
He had been bitten by black cobras in hundreds of deserted temples that had been turned into beds;
his head had been crushed hundreds of times by falling from the tops of bilva trees;
and his cheeks had been repeatedly scarred by the claws of bears dwelling in ruined shrines dedicated to the divine mothers.
He was constantly mocked by people engaged in springtime festivities who would lift up broken pieces of furniture and place them upon an old female slave as if she were a bride;

he endured fruitless rising from his bed after lying down in many different dwellings; and even in his state of extreme wretchedness, he bore his own family, though surrounded by various diseases, as if they were his own kin.

He displayed even his folly as if it had given birth to many offspring, for it was followed by numerous calamities; he manifested even his anger as if it were bearing fruit, for it produced many swellings on his limbs from the blows of various staffs and strikes; and he made even his suffering appear as if it had many mouths, for it was revealed through the burns and wounds caused by lamps whose flames touched every part of his body.

Bearing, as it were, a continuous flood of hundreds of kicks delivered by the people of the countryside— consisting of groundless insults and verbal abuse— he carried a large, well-made basket fashioned from dry forest creepers.

He saw Caṇḍikā presided over by an aged Dravidian ascetic, who carried a hook for dislodging flowers fashioned from a bamboo cane, and who was never for a moment without his black woolen blanket draped over his shoulder.
And he chose to take up residence right there.

Then, having dismounted from his horse and entered, he bowed down to her with a mind inclined toward devotion. Having performed a circumambulation and bowed once more, as he wandered about out of curiosity to see that peaceful region, he heard one shouting loudly and crying out in anger.
In one part, he saw a Dravidian ascetic;
upon seeing him, although he was tormented by the longing and agitation of separation from Kādambarī,
he laughed for a long time and restrained those who had begun a quarrel with him.
As his own soldiers were mocking him,
he somehow brought them to a state of calm through soothing words and hundreds of conciliatory, affectionate speeches; then, in due order,
he himself questioned them regarding their birthplace, caste, learning, wives, children, wealth, age, and the reason for their renunciation.
When questioned, he described himself;

and as he became eloquent in recounting his past valor, beauty, and wealth, the prince grew exceedingly fond of him. His life story served, as it were, to provide diversion for the prince’s heart, which was distressed by separation.
Having developed a sense of familiarity, he had betel offered to him.
And when the Blessed Sun, the seven-horsed charioteer, had set,
the princes took up residence beneath the trees as they were available.

When the horses had been tethered with golden saddles hung from the branches; when they were dusty from rolling on the surface of the earth and their energy was inferred by the shaking of their manes; when they had taken a few mouthfuls of young grass and drunk water; when their fatigue had vanished because their backs were still wet from bathing; and when they were secured with spears driven into the ground before them.
When the soldiers, exhausted by the day’s journey, were about to sleep upon beds of leaves arranged near their horses— having turned over their sentries—
and while the military camp shone as if it were still day, the darkness having been swallowed by the light of many fires, Candrāpīḍa was [separated] from his attendants in one corner.

He went to the bed prepared before him by Indrāyudha, which had been announced by the chamberlain (*pratīhāra*). As soon as he was seated, a sense of distress touched his heart; seized by restlessness, he dismissed the circle of courtiers.
He did not speak even to those standing by his side, though they were most dear to him;
with eyes closed, he repeatedly traveled in his mind to the land of the Kimpuruṣas;
with undivided attention, he remembered Hemakūṭa; and filled with longing, he thought:

Feeling a causeless longing, he thought: disregarding his kinship with the venerable Mahāśvetā and her favors, he longed for the sight of Kādambarī again and again as the very fruit of his life; and he intensely desired the acquaintance of Madalekhā, who was charmingly free from pride.
He longed to see Tamālikā, anticipated Keyūraka’s arrival,
and beheld the ice-house.

On the couch, he sighed hotly and repeatedly, and again and again he let out a long breath; he felt a greater affection for Śeṣahārā than for his kinsmen, and later he considered Patralekhā, who stood nearby, to be a partaker of his merit, and thus, without even falling asleep, he passed that night with her.
The merchant, having risen at the will of that aged Dravidian devotee— having fulfilled his desire with vast outpourings of wealth bestowed according to his own wish—
dwelt for some days in regions that were both beloved and exceedingly delightful, and thus arrived at Ujjayinī.
Receiving thousands of salutations with palms joined like precious lotuses from the citizens, who were both delighted and bewildered by his sudden arrival, he entered the city unexpectedly.

And from his retinue, who were rushing forward in a frantic scramble out of an excess of joy, he learned: "My Lord, Candrāpīḍa is at the door. Upon hearing this, his father—moving with a gait slow from the weight of intense bliss, like Mount Mandara drawing up the waters of the Ocean of Milk while trailing its pure silken upper garment;
raining down drops of tears from eyes overflowing with joy, like the celestial Kalpa-tree showering a downpour of loosened pearls—approached.
He was followed by those standing nearby— men with hair grey from old age, anointed with sandalwood paste, wearing unblemished linen garments,

and adorned with bracelets, turbans, crowns, and floral crests— who made the earth appear as if it possessed many Mount Kailāsas and many Oceans of Milk, and who carried swords, canes, umbrellas, banners, and yak-tail whisks.

He went forth to meet him on foot with thousands of kings. And Candrāpīḍa, having seen his father from afar, dismounted from his horse and touched the earth with his head, which was garlanded by the rays of his crest-jewel.

Then, having called out with outstretched arms, "Come, come!"— having been summoned with great affection and embraced firmly for a long time by his father, and having offered salutations to the venerable ministers and kings present at that time, the king took him by the hand and led him to the palace of Vilāsavatī.

He too was greeted with joy by her as she emerged from the entire retinue of the inner apartments; having been welcomed and his arrival celebrated, he performed the auspicious rites for his arrival and, after staying for some time engaged in conversations related to his world-conquest, went to see Śukanāsa. There also, remaining for a very long time in that same manner, he reported that Vaiśampāyana was well and had set out from the military camp.
Having beheld Manoramā,
he returned to the palace of Vilāsavatī and, as if under another's influence, completed all his daily duties such as bathing;
in the afternoon, he went to his own residence.
There, his mind tormented by longing, he considered not only himself, but his own palace, the city of Avanti, and indeed the entire circle of the earth, as empty without Kādambarī.

Then, eager to hear news of the Gandharva king’s daughter, he awaited Patralekhā’s arrival as if it were a great festival, a time for obtaining a desired boon, or the moment of the birth of the nectar of immortality.
After several days had passed, Meghanāda arrived, bringing Patralekhā with him.
And he brought her forward;

then Candrāpīḍa, having offered his salutations from afar, with a smile revealing his affection, rose and embraced Patralekhā— who, though naturally dear to him, had now attained a state of even greater endearment as if she had acquired a further fortune of favor through Kādambarī— embracing her with an exceeding display of respect.
And he touched Meghanāda, who was bowing before him, with his sprout-like hand.
Having sat down, he said to her as she sat beside him: “Patralekhā!”
"Tell me, is all the retinue— Tamālikā, Keyūraka, and the others— well, including the noble Mahāśvetā, Queen Samadalekhā, and Princess Kādambarī?
She replied, "O King," and so on.
"As you command, blessed one!
Princess Kādambarī, together with her circle of friends and her attendants, honors you with her hands joined in reverence held above her head.
Having spoken thus, he took Patralekhā and entered the interior of the palace, leaving behind the royal retinue.
And there, his mind burning with curiosity and unable to restrain himself,
he pushed back his attendants with great affection and entered; there he saw a land-lotus plant that had recently sprouted within the house, for which the broad,
upturned stalks and leaves had performed the function of a royal parasol.

Having occupied one half of the couch in a leaf-pavilion—which, like a bed-chamber, resembled an emerald banner—he sat down at the foot of a palm tree, having gently nudged with his lotus-foot a pair of swans that were sleeping soundly there. Then he asked: "Patralekhā, tell me, how have you been staying since I departed?"

For how many days? Or who remembers us with such intensity? [That is: "Who remembers you with such intensity," or "Who has a greater affection for you"? Or for whom is there a greater affection? [In this context, the reading "for me" (*mayi*) is additionally inserted. It is said: "for whom there is a greater affection."
Thus questioned, she replied: "Your Majesty,
listen with attention to how I am situated."
For as many days as there were, of whatever nature was the favor of the goddess, and in what manner the assemblies took place—
And such were the conversations that arose:
"Who remembers you with the greatest intensity?
or "Who has the most profound affection for you?"
Then, indeed, when the King had departed, I returned with Keyūraka and sat down right there near the bed of flowers, just as before;
and I remained there at ease, experiencing ever-new favors from the Queen. What need is there for more? For the most part, her eye was my eye.
Beauty upon the body,
a sprout-like hand in the hand,
and arrows within the syllables of her name.

Her heart filled with joy, she spent that entire day in love; and in the afternoon, leaning upon me alone, she emerged from the winter-house and, wandering at her pleasure while keeping her attendants behind her, went to the beloved children’s garden.
There, she ascended the middle of the terrace of the pleasure grove, which was white as plaster and seemed as if made of the waves of the Yamunā’s waters by means of its flight of emerald steps.
Leaning against a jeweled pillar within it, she stood gazing [at me]; and having remained there for what seemed like a moment,

yet in truth for a long time, as if deliberating with her heart what something might be said, she gazed at my face for a very long while with eyes whose pupils were fixed and whose lashes were motionless.
Gazing [at him] and looking [upon him], having formed a resolve and desiring to enter the fire of passion, she trembled as if being carried away by a torrent in the stream of her perspiration;
and with her limbs trembling, she was seized by despair as if she were about to fall.

Then, having discerned his intention, I fixed my steady gaze upon his face and gave it my full attention; when I had thus requested, "Command me," she seemed as if restrained even by her own trembling limbs.
Out of shame at hearing the secret, she touched even her own reflection—my likeness—drawn upon the jeweled floor with her big toe, as if to drive it away.
With her lotus-foot, its anklets jingling as they scraped the floor, she sent forth the palace swans.
She drove away even the bees from her ear-lotuses with the perspiring breath exhaled from her fanning face;
she offered a fragment of betel-roll, bitten by her teeth as if it were a bribe, to the peacock;
and she looked here and there again and again, as if fearing that the forest deities might overhear her.

Though she desired to speak, she was unable to utter even a single word, her voice faltering and choked with shame; and though she strove to do so, she seemed utterly consumed by the blazing fire of passion,
as if carried away by the flowing torrent of her tears.
She was as if overwhelmed by sorrows entering her,
as if shattered into pieces by falling arrows of the flower-bowed god,
and as if pinned down by sighs issuing forth.
As if expelled by her sighs,
as if held captive by hundreds of anxieties dwelling within her heart, and as if swallowed up by her breaths.
Her speech did not flow forth, as if it were being drunk up by swarms of bees in the form of her sighs; she merely fashioned,

as it were, a rosary of pearls for counting her thousands of sorrows, displaying a gloomy day with pure teardrops falling downward from her cheeks, untouched by them, as she sat with her face cast down.
And then, as if learning from her, even bashfulness learned bashfulness, grace learned grace, and even discipline learned the instruction of discipline; bashfulness learned the grace of bashfulness,
discipline learned an excellence of discipline, and even simplicity learned simplicity.
Even cleverness is cleverness,
fear is timidity, and even confusion is the state of being bewildered.
Even her despondency was despondent, and even her grace was graceful;
and thus she appeared, O Queen.

When I asked, "What is this?", she wiped her eyes, which were reddening in their centers, and with an intensity of grief that seemed as if to hang herself, she grasped with her vine-like arm— tender as a lotus stalk— the flower garland woven by the maidens of the altar.
With one raised eyebrow, she gazed as if at the path of death or the noose of Yama, sighing long and hot.

As she contemplated that sorrow, she was repeatedly urged by me to speak of its cause; yet, out of shame, scratching the petals of a *ketakī* flower with her fingernails as if she were writing down what she had to say, her lower lip quivering with the desire to speak, whispering as if to bees drawn by her sighs, she remained for a long time with her eyes fixed motionlessly upon the surface of the earth.

Gradually, fixing her gaze once more upon my face, she again filled her eyes with tears; then, as if washing away her speech—which had been greyed by the smoke of the fire of passion—with the drops of tear-water falling from her overflowing eyes, she somehow turned herself toward me.

She did so while, through the shimmering rays of her teeth flashing in an embarrassed smile, she seemed to string together, under the guise of those very teardrops, the previously forgotten syllables of her message that she had failed to utter due to her agitation.
And she said to me, “Patralekhā,
because of my affection for you, neither my father, nor my mother, nor Mahāśvetā, nor Madalekhā, nor even my own life is as dear to me in that place as you have been since the moment I beheld you.”
I do not know for what reason my heart, having cast aside all its circle of female friends, places its trust in you; it sighs [in despair].
Whom else shall I blame, or to whom else shall I tell of this humiliation?
With whom else can I share this suffering? Having reported this unbearable burden of sorrow to you, I shall give up my life;
I swear it to you by my very life.
I am ashamed even by my own heart, which knows this occurrence,
let alone by the hearts of others.
How indeed could one such as I stain with the scandal of ill repute a family as pure as the rays of the moon?

She will abandon the modesty inherited through her family lineage, and her mind will incline toward the restlessness that is unbecoming of a maiden— or rather, appropriate for other maidens and for other young women.
I was not intended [in marriage] by my father, nor was I given away by my mother; and thus, being neither intended by my father nor given away by my mother,
I was not approved by my elders.
Therefore, I send no message, I dispatch nothing,
and I show no outward sign.
Like one who is timid, like one who is helpless, like one who is lowly— indeed, brought by the prince Candrāpīḍa, who was both arrogant and overbearing, to a state of profound reproach;
tell me, is this the conduct of the great?
Is this the fruit of familiarity, that my mind—so delicate as the fiber of a fresh lotus stalk—is thus being insulted?
For young maidens are not to be treated with contempt by youths; indeed, they are not to be overcome.
Generally, the fire of passion first burns away shame, and then the heart;
first, the arrows of the flower-bowed god shatter modesty and the like.
Afterwards, [he said]:
"I bid you farewell for our meeting again in another future birth; for there is no end dearer to me than you."
"I shall wash away my own stain by means of the penance of renouncing my life.
Having said this, he became silent.

But I, for my part—truly, because I was unaware of what had transpired—felt as if I were carried away, as if terrified, as if embarrassed, and as if deprived of my senses; thus, with despondency, I addressed him: "O Queen!"
I wish to hear;
command me, what was done by Your Majesty Candrāpīḍa, or what offense has occurred?
"By whom indeed has the Queen’s mind, which is naturally gentle as a white water-lily and undeserving of distress, been so troubled by such lack of discipline?
Having first heard that I have surrendered my life, the Queen will afterwards surrender her own life"—thinking thus, [he said], "I shall give up my life;
she will give up her life."
Having been addressed thus, she spoke again: “I inform you;
listen attentively. Every single day, coming repeatedly in my dreams, a clever rogue, skilled in messages, makes the parrot and the maina in their cages his messengers.”
And he uses a *sārikā* bird as a messenger.
With his mind deluded by futile desires for her who is asleep, he writes messages regarding places of assignation upon the inner surfaces of her earrings and ivory bracelets.

Although the characters have been washed away by perspiration, they remain beautiful and reveal his own condition through rows of tear-drops mixed with collyrium that have fallen [upon them], following the course of his infatuation and hope.
He sends love-letters;
he forcibly dyes his feet with red lac as if with the essence of his own passion;
unconscious due to immodesty, he holds himself in high esteem when his own reflection is mirrored in his nails.
In the groves, as she fled alone out of fear of being seized, her progress hindered by the hem of her garment caught in the foliage,

he— feigning boldness— embraced her as if she had been captured; and though she turned her face away, he performed an embrace while she was being presented by her creeper-friends as if she were his own.
Drawing a leaf-pattern upon my breast, he— whose nature is crooked as if teaching his naturally simple mind the ways of guile—

fans my cheeks with breezes from his mouth that are cool as if they were the winds from the waves of longing in his heart, and which are starred with droplets of perspiration. Though his grip has loosened due to the moisture of sweat and he has lost his blue lotuses, this wretched fellow, with his hand, gathers the pure rays of his nails like sprouts of barley, pressing them against the hollows of my ears.

Having repeatedly seized me by the hair, he playfully forces me to drink mouthfuls of wine that he has already swallowed during the time of watering his most beloved young *bakula* trees; thus, with his movements counted by his grip on my hair, he makes me drink.
Deceived by his own wicked intellect, he receives upon his head the kicks of my feet as I am intent on striking the *aśoka* tree of the palace.

As if lifting an upper garment with her network of bristling hair, and as if untying from her neck a necklace composed of moonbeams— clinging to the tips of the crocodiles on the jeweled filigree of her swaying earrings— which was like a noose placed there by the god of love for the sake of death, she,
though her heart was overwhelmed with joy, assumed the innate modesty of a maiden and spoke very slowly: "I acknowledge your great affection..."
How could women possess such boldness, especially young maidens who, by their very nature, are as delicate as the soft petals of the unhardened *śirīṣa* flower? They were merely her accomplices.
Those who send messages themselves or approach me of their own accord— I shrink from a foolish woman who sends such a bold message herself.
What more shall I say? To say "you are very dear" is a tautology;
to say "I am your beloved self" is the question of a fool.

"Your passion for me is profound"—this is the speech of a courtesan; "I cannot live without you"—this is a contradiction of one's own words; "Love overcomes me"—this is a reproach for one's own faults.
"I have been given to you by the god of love" is a means of approaching;
"You were carried off by me by force" is the audacity of a harlot;
"You must certainly come" is the pride of her own good fortune.

"I am coming myself" is the fickleness of a woman; "this man is devoted to no other" is the rashness of proclaiming one's own devotion; "I will not send a message for fear of being rejected" is the awakening of one who is already awake; and "disregard for the suffering of those who depend on me" is cruel.
"That you shall know joy in death is indeed impossible. Thus ends the first part of the *Kādambarī* composed by the illustrious Bāṇabhaṭṭa.
